26: That a man's life is only a dream — many have guessed at that before me, and the feeling follows me everywhere too.
Consider how narrow the limits are that confine our active, inquiring powers.
Consider how all our energy is spent providing for bare necessities, which in turn have no end beyond prolonging a wretched existence.

Consider how all our satisfaction on certain questions of enquiry comes to nothing better than a passive resignation, while we amuse ourselves painting our prison walls with bright figures and brilliant landscapes.
When I consider all of it, Wilhelm, I fall silent.
I examine my own being and find a world there — but a world of imagination and dim desire rather than of clear outline and living power.
Then everything swims before my senses, and I go on my way through the world smiling and dreaming.
27: All the learned professors and doctors agree that children do not understand the cause of their own desires.

But that grown men should wander this earth like children, not knowing where they come from or where they are going, moved as little by settled motives, and steered just as children are by biscuits and sugar-plums and the rod — that is what nobody is willing to admit.
And yet I think it is plain enough.
28: I know what you will say in reply, and I am ready to grant it: the happiest people are those who live like children.
They amuse themselves with their playthings, dress and undress their dolls, and keep a careful watch on the cupboard where mother has locked up the sweet things.
And when they finally get a delicious mouthful, they eat it greedily and cry, "More!"

But there are others to envy as well — those who dress up their paltry occupations, and sometimes even their passions, in grand titles, and present them to the world as gigantic achievements performed for its welfare and glory.
But then there is the man who humbly recognises how empty all this is.

He sees with what pleasure the thriving townsman turns his little garden into a paradise, and how patiently even the poor man goes his weary way under his burden, and how all of them wish equally to see the light of the sun a little longer.
That man is at peace, and makes his own world within himself; and he too is happy, because he is a man.
And then, however narrow his sphere, he still keeps in his heart the sweet feeling of liberty, and knows he can leave this prison whenever he chooses.
30: You know my old way of settling anywhere — picking out a little cottage in some snug spot and putting up with every inconvenience in it.
Here too I have found such a comfortable place, one that holds a peculiar charm for me.
31: About a league from the town is a place called Walheim.
(The reader need not go to the trouble of looking for it: we have found it necessary to change the names given in the original.)
It lies beautifully on the side of a hill, and if you follow one of the footpaths out of the village you can look out over the whole valley.
A good old woman lives there who keeps a small inn.
She sells wine, beer, and coffee, and for all her age she is cheerful and pleasant.
The great charm of the place is two linden-trees, spreading their enormous branches over the little green in front of the church, which is ringed about with peasants' cottages, barns, and farmyards.
I have seldom seen a spot so quiet and so much its own.
I often have my table and chair carried out from the little inn, and drink my coffee there and read my Homer.
Chance brought me there one fine afternoon, and I found the place completely deserted.
Everyone was in the fields except a little boy of about four, who sat on the ground holding a baby of six months between his knees.
He pressed it to his chest with both arms, so that he made a kind of armchair for it; and for all the liveliness sparkling in its black eyes, the baby stayed perfectly still.
The sight delighted me.
I sat down on a plough opposite them and sketched this little picture of brotherly tenderness with great pleasure.
I added the hedge nearby, the barn door, and some broken cart-wheels, just as they happened to lie.
After about an hour I found I had made a drawing that was accurate and full of interest, without having put in the slightest thing of my own.
That confirmed me in my resolve to hold, from now on, entirely to nature.
She alone is inexhaustible, and she alone can form a great master.
Much can be said for rules, just as much can be said for the laws of society.

An artist trained on them will never produce anything downright bad or disgusting, just as a man who keeps the law and observes decorum can never be a wholly intolerable neighbour or an outright villain.
But say what you like about rules: they destroy the genuine feeling of nature, and its true expression with it.
Do not tell me that this is too hard, that rules only restrain and prune away superfluous branches, etc.
My good friend, let me put it to you by way of a comparison.
These things are like love.
A warm-hearted young man attaches himself deeply to a girl.
He spends every hour of the day in her company, wears out his health, and squanders his fortune, all to prove at every moment that he is wholly hers.
Then along comes a man of the world, a man of position and respectability, who says to him: "My good young friend, love is natural; but you must love within bounds.
Divide your time: give a part of it to business, and keep your hours of recreation for your mistress.
Reckon up your fortune, and out of what is left over you may make her a present — only not too often; on her birthday, and such occasions."
If he follows this advice, he may turn into a useful member of society, and I would advise any prince to give him a post.
But it is all over with his love — and with his genius, if he is an artist.
Oh, my friend! Why is it that the torrent of genius so seldom bursts out, so seldom comes rolling down in full flood to overwhelm your astonished soul?
Because on both banks of that stream live cool and respectable people, whose summer-houses and tulip-beds would suffer from a flood.
So they dig their trenches and raise their embankments in good time, to head off the danger before it comes.
33: I find I have fallen into raptures and declamation and similes, and so forgotten to tell you what became of the children.
Absorbed in the artistic contemplations I sketched for you in yesterday's letter, I went on sitting on that plough for two hours.
Toward evening a young woman came running toward the children with a basket on her arm.
They had not moved the whole time.
She called out while she was still some way off, "You are a good boy, Philip!"
She greeted me; I returned it, got up, and went over to her.
I asked whether she was the mother of those pretty children.
"Yes," she said; and giving the eldest a piece of bread, she took the baby in her arms and kissed it with a mother's tenderness.
"I left my child in Philip's care," she said, "while I went into town with my eldest boy to buy some wheat bread, some sugar, and an earthen pot."
I could see the various things in the basket; the cover had slipped off.
"I am going to make some broth tonight for my little Hans," she said.
"That wild fellow, the big one, broke my pot yesterday, scrambling with Philip over what was left in it."
I asked after the eldest, and she had hardly had time to tell me he was driving a couple of geese home from the meadow when he came running up and handed Philip a willow switch.
I talked a little longer with the woman and learned that she was the schoolmaster's daughter, and that her husband had gone off to Switzerland to collect some money a relative had left him.
"They meant to cheat him," she said, "and would not answer his letters, so he has gone there himself.
I hope nothing has happened to him; I have heard nothing since he left."
I was sorry to leave the woman.
I gave each of the children a kreutzer, and one more for the youngest, to buy him some wheat bread for his broth the next time she went to town; and so we parted.
I tell you, my dear friend, when my thoughts are all in turmoil, the sight of a creature like this settles my troubled mind.
She moves in a happy thoughtlessness inside the narrow circle of her life, supplying her wants from one day to the next.
And when she sees the leaves falling, it raises no thought in her but that winter is coming.
Since then I have gone out there often.
The children are quite used to me now.
Each of them gets a lump of sugar when I drink my coffee, and in the evening they share my bread and butter and milk.
They always get their kreutzer on Sundays, since the good woman has orders to give it to them whenever I am not there after evening service.
They are entirely at home with me and tell me everything.
I am particularly amused by their tempers, and by how simply they behave when some of the other village children are gathered with them.
34: It has cost me a good deal of trouble to quiet the mother's anxiety.
She is afraid, as she puts it, that "they should inconvenience the gentleman."
36: What I said lately about painting holds just as true of poetry.
All we need is to recognise what is really excellent, and to dare to give it expression — and that is a great deal said in few words.
Today I had a scene which, set down just as it happened, would make the most beautiful idyll in the world.
But why talk of poetry and scenes and idylls?
Can we never take pleasure in nature without having to fall back on art?
37: If you are expecting anything grand or magnificent after that introduction, you will be badly disappointed.
It concerns nothing more than a peasant lad who has stirred the warmest interest in me.
As usual I shall tell the story badly, and as usual you will think me extravagant.
It is Walheim again — always Walheim — that produces these wonders.
38: A party had gathered outside the house under the linden-trees to drink coffee.
The company did not quite suit me, and on one pretext or another I hung back.
39: A peasant came out of a house nearby and set to work on part of the same plough I had sketched not long before.
I liked the look of him.
I spoke to him, asked about his circumstances, made his acquaintance, and — as usually happens between me and people of that class — was soon taken into his confidence.
He told me he was in the service of a young widow who thought highly of him.
He spoke so much about his mistress, and praised her so extravagantly, that I could soon see he was desperately in love with her.
"She is no longer young," he said.
"She was treated so badly by her first husband that she does not mean to marry again."
From the way he spoke it was plain what incomparable charms she had for him.
It was plain how fiercely he wished she would choose him, and wipe out the memory of her first husband's misconduct.
To convey the depth of the poor fellow's attachment, his truthfulness and devotion, I would have to repeat his own words.
It would take a great poet to render the look on his face, the harmony of his voice, the heavenly fire in his eye.
No words of mine can catch the tenderness of his every movement and every expression; no effort of mine could do the scene justice.
What touched me most was his fear that I might misunderstand his position with regard to his mistress, or doubt the propriety of her conduct.

The charm with which he described her figure and her person — which, without the graces of youth, had taken hold of him and bound him to her — cannot be put into words, and must be left to the imagination.
Never in my life have I witnessed, or imagined, or thought possible, such intense devotion, such ardent affection, joined with so much purity.
Do not blame me if I say that the memory of this innocence and truth is stamped deep into my soul.
This picture of fidelity and tenderness follows me everywhere.
And my own heart, as though kindled at that flame, glows and burns within me.
40: I mean to try to see her as soon as I can.
Or perhaps, on second thoughts, I had better not: better that I should see her through her lover's eyes.
Seen with my own, she might not appear as she now stands before me — and why should I spoil so sweet a picture?
